crystal.name: Crystal structures and Miller indices
crystal.description: Check the coordination numbers and packing factors of SC, BCC, FCC and HCP, densities calculated from the unit cell, and Miller indices and interplanar spacings with multiple-choice questions. A numerical way to firm up the basics of crystallography.
crystal.intro:
Most metals take one of three crystal structures: body-centered cubic (BCC), face-centered cubic (FCC) or hexagonal close-packed (HCP). The coordination number is 8 for BCC and 12 for FCC and HCP, and the atomic packing factor is about 0.68 for BCC and about 0.74 for FCC and HCP. Knowing the number of atoms per unit cell (2 for BCC, 4 for FCC) and the lattice parameter, you can calculate the density.
Crystal planes and directions are described by Miller indices. The indices of a plane are the reciprocals of its intercepts on the axes, reduced to the smallest integer ratio. In cubic crystals the interplanar spacing is d = a/√(h² + k² + l²), and the [hkl] direction is perpendicular to the (hkl) plane. These are the foundation for understanding slip systems and XRD peaks.

defects-diffusion.name: Crystal defects and diffusion
defects-diffusion.description: Learn the Arrhenius expression for vacancy concentration, dislocations and the Burgers vector, grain boundaries, Fick's laws, diffusion coefficients and the error-function solution with multiple-choice questions, including practice calculations for carburizing and dopant diffusion.
defects-diffusion.intro:
Real crystals contain point defects such as vacancies and interstitials, line defects called dislocations, and planar defects such as grain boundaries. The vacancy concentration rises steeply with temperature following exp(−Q/kT), and vacancies carry diffusion. Dislocations are characterized by the Burgers vector, which is perpendicular to the dislocation line for an edge dislocation and parallel to it for a screw dislocation.
Diffusion is described by Fick's laws; at steady state the flux is proportional to the concentration gradient. The diffusion coefficient depends strongly on temperature through D = D₀exp(−Q/RT), and √(Dt) gives a rough diffusion distance. When the surface concentration is held constant, as in carburizing, the error-function solution relates depth and time.

mechanical.name: Mechanical properties and fracture
mechanical.description: Check stress–strain curves, Young's modulus, 0.2% offset yield strength, true stress, hardness testing, fracture toughness, fatigue, creep and the ductile-to-brittle transition with multiple-choice questions, and practice strength-design calculations with explanations.
mechanical.intro:
The stress–strain curve from a tensile test gives Young's modulus, the yield stress (or 0.2% offset yield strength), the tensile strength and the elongation. Young's modulus is set by interatomic bonding and hardly changes with heat treatment, whereas the yield stress varies greatly with microstructure. Make sure you also know the difference between engineering and true stress, and the principles of the Vickers, Brinell and Rockwell hardness tests.
In real fracture, the critical stress or crack length is estimated from the crack size and the fracture toughness K_IC using K = Yσ√(πa). Fatigue under cyclic loading, creep that progresses over time at high temperature, and the ductile-to-brittle transition that embrittles BCC metals at low temperature are also key phenomena that govern the life of components.

phase-diagram.name: Phase diagrams and the lever rule
phase-diagram.description: Check Gibbs' phase rule, isomorphous, eutectic and peritectic phase diagrams, phase and microconstituent fractions by the lever rule, and the essentials of the Fe-C diagram with multiple-choice questions, and practice fraction calculations with explanations.
phase-diagram.intro:
A phase diagram shows which phases exist at equilibrium as a function of temperature and composition. For a binary system at constant pressure the phase rule becomes F = C − P + 1, so eutectic and eutectoid points, where three phases coexist, are invariant points with zero degrees of freedom. Learn to read the basic types: isomorphous systems such as Cu-Ni, eutectic systems such as Pb-Sn, and peritectic systems in which liquid and solid react.
In a two-phase region, the ends of the tie line give the composition of each phase and the lever rule gives the fraction of each phase. In the Fe-Fe₃C system, the eutectoid reaction at 0.76 wt% C and 727 °C produces pearlite; proeutectoid ferrite appears in hypoeutectoid steels and proeutectoid cementite in hypereutectoid steels. The key is to distinguish phases from microconstituents when calculating fractions.

heat-treatment.name: Heat treatment and metallic materials
heat-treatment.description: Learn TTT and CCT diagrams, martensite, quenching and tempering, precipitation hardening, solid-solution strengthening, the Hall–Petch relation, and the basics of steels and aluminum alloys with multiple-choice questions.
heat-treatment.intro:
Heat treatment of steel is the art of producing different microstructures by controlling how fast austenite is cooled. Cooling faster than the nose of the TTT or CCT diagram produces martensite by a diffusionless, shear-type transformation. Martensite is hard and brittle, so it is tempered to restore toughness before use. Alloying elements shift the nose to longer times and raise hardenability.
Metals are strengthened by solid-solution strengthening, work hardening, grain refinement (the Hall–Petch relation) and precipitation hardening. In alloys such as Al-Cu, fine precipitates formed by solution treatment, quenching and aging give large strengthening, but aging too long softens the alloy by overaging. Make sure you know which strengthening mechanisms are used in which alloys.

ceramics.name: Ceramics and glasses
ceramics.description: Check ionic bonding and coordination numbers, representative crystal structures, sintering, the glass transition, strength scatter by Weibull statistics, thermal shock, and dielectric and piezoelectric materials with multiple-choice questions, including calculations with explanations.
ceramics.intro:
Most ceramics are held together by ionic or covalent bonds, and the coordination number of the cation is roughly determined by the cation-to-anion radius ratio. Learn the structures and coordination numbers of types such as NaCl, CsCl and perovskite. Sintering, in which powders are consolidated at high temperature, is driven by the reduction in surface energy.
Ceramics fail in a brittle manner from small internal flaws, so their strength scatters widely and the probability of failure is evaluated with the Weibull distribution. Glass is a supercooled liquid whose structure has frozen in, and its glass transition temperature depends on the cooling rate. Ferroelectrics such as BaTiO₃ are indispensable in electronic components as capacitors and piezoelectric elements.

polymers.name: Polymers and composites
polymers.description: Learn the types of polymerization, molecular weight and its distribution, crystallinity, the glass transition temperature, viscoelastic models, thermoplastics versus thermosets, and the rule of mixtures and critical fiber length with multiple-choice questions, with practice calculations and explanations.
polymers.intro:
Polymers consist of long molecular chains in which monomers are linked by addition or condensation polymerization. Molecular weight has a distribution, and the ratio of the weight-average molecular weight Mw to the number-average molecular weight Mn indicates its breadth. In crystalline polymers, which mix crystalline and amorphous regions, the crystallinity governs density, stiffness and transparency, and the temperature at which molecular motion in the amorphous regions freezes is the glass transition temperature Tg.
Polymer deformation is viscoelastic, depending on time and temperature, and stress relaxation and creep are represented by the Maxwell and Voigt models. The stiffness of fiber-reinforced composites is estimated by the isostrain rule of mixtures along the fibers and the isostress rule perpendicular to them, and for short fibers the critical fiber length determines the reinforcing effect.

electronic-materials.name: Electronic, magnetic and optical materials
electronic-materials.description: Check the basics of band theory, the conductivity of metals and semiconductors, Matthiessen's rule, the Hall effect, ferromagnetism and hysteresis, soft and hard magnetic materials, and refraction, absorption and emission with multiple-choice questions.
electronic-materials.intro:
The electrical properties of materials can be understood through band structure. Metals conduct well because there are continuous empty levels at the Fermi level, and their resistivity increases with temperature as scattering by lattice vibrations grows. In semiconductors, doping can change the conductivity σ = neμ enormously, and in the intrinsic regime the resistivity falls as temperature rises. The resistivity of metals is split into lattice-vibration and impurity components by Matthiessen's rule.
Ferromagnets have a spontaneous magnetization below the Curie temperature, and the shape of the hysteresis loop determines their applications. Soft magnetic materials with low coercivity are used for transformer and motor cores, and hard magnetic materials with high coercivity for permanent magnets. Among optical properties, the refractive index and reflectance, the absorption coefficient, and the difference between direct and indirect transitions are important.

thin-films.name: Thin films, surfaces and nanomaterials
thin-films.description: Learn surface energy, homogeneous and heterogeneous nucleation and the critical nucleus radius, thin-film growth modes, thermal stress in films, and the characteristics of nanomaterials such as specific surface area and the quantum size effect with multiple-choice questions.
thin-films.intro:
Atoms at surfaces and interfaces have lost some of their bonds and so carry excess energy (surface energy and interfacial energy). When a nucleus of a new phase forms, the decrease in volume free energy competes with the increase in interfacial energy, and only nuclei larger than the critical radius r* = −2γ/ΔGv grow. Heterogeneous nucleation on substrates and walls has a lower energy barrier.
Thin films grow in layer-by-layer, island, or layer-then-island modes, depending on the balance of surface energies and the lattice mismatch. The difference in thermal expansion from the substrate produces a thermal stress σ = EΔαΔT/(1 − ν), which causes bowing, delamination and interconnect failures. Making particles nanosized increases the specific surface area, and the quantum size effect and Ostwald ripening become prominent.

characterization.name: Materials characterization (SEM, TEM, XRD, XPS)
characterization.description: Check Bragg's law, extinction rules and lattice parameters for cubic crystals, the Scherrer equation, secondary and backscattered electrons in SEM, EDS and WDS, TEM, XPS, SIMS, and DSC and TGA with multiple-choice questions.
characterization.intro:
In XRD, interplanar spacings are found from Bragg's law 2d sinθ = nλ, and for cubic crystals the extinction rules (h + k + l even for BCC; h, k and l all even or all odd for FCC) are used to index peaks and determine lattice parameters. Peak widths give an estimate of crystallite size through the Scherrer equation.
In electron microscopy, SEM secondary electron images show surface shape, backscattered electron images show compositional differences, and EDS or WDS analyzes the elements present. TEM observes the internal crystal structure and defects in thin lamellae. The chemical state of surfaces is examined by XPS, depth profiles of trace elements by SIMS, and thermal changes by DSC and TGA. Knowing how the techniques differ in information depth and sensitivity is the key to choosing among them in failure analysis.

metals.name: Metals and alloys
metals.description: Check carbon steel designations, the types of stainless steel, the characteristics of aluminum, titanium and copper alloys, solid-solution strengthening and work hardening, recovery and recrystallization, and solidification structures of castings with multiple-choice questions, and practice calculations of specific strength and solidification time.
metals.intro:
Steel is the mainstay of engineering metals. In carbon steels, the carbon content sets the balance between hardness and ductility, and designations such as S45C (JIS) indicate the carbon content. Stainless steels, containing about 11% Cr or more, are divided by microstructure into austenitic, ferritic and martensitic grades, which differ in magnetism and in whether they harden on quenching. Among nonferrous metals, organize light aluminum alloys, titanium alloys with excellent specific strength and corrosion resistance, and readily worked copper alloys by alloy system and designation.
The basic way to strengthen a metal is to obstruct dislocation motion. Typical methods are solid-solution strengthening by interstitial or substitutional solute atoms and work hardening, which multiplies dislocations by cold working; when a work-hardened metal is heated, it changes through recovery, recrystallization and grain growth in that order. Hot and cold working are distinguished by the recrystallization temperature. In castings, chill grains, columnar grains and equiaxed grains form in that order from the mold wall, and the solidification time can be estimated with Chvorinov's rule.

corrosion.name: Corrosion and surface treatment
corrosion.description: Check standard electrode potentials, local cells and differential aeration cells, galvanic corrosion, passivity, pitting and stress corrosion cracking, and protection by sacrificial anodes, plating and painting with multiple-choice questions, and practice calculating corrosion amounts with Faraday's law.
corrosion.intro:
Corrosion of metals is an electrochemical reaction that proceeds as a pair: an anodic reaction in which the metal gives up electrons and becomes cations, and a cathodic reaction in which dissolved oxygen or hydrogen ions accept electrons. Metals with more active standard electrode potentials tend to dissolve more readily. Even on the surface of a single metal, nonuniformities and oxygen concentration differences create local cells, and when dissimilar metals are in contact, galvanic corrosion occurs in which the more active one dissolves faster.
Stainless steels and titanium are protected by passive films a few nanometers thick, but localized corrosion requires care: pitting and crevice corrosion caused by chloride ions, and stress corrosion cracking when tensile stress and environment coincide. Protection methods include sacrificial anodes, plating and painting, and the key point is how active zinc protects steel. Amounts of corrosion and plating can be calculated from current and time with Faraday's law.

energy-materials.name: Battery and energy materials
energy-materials.description: Check cathode and anode materials for lithium-ion batteries and theoretical capacity calculations, layered, spinel and olivine structures, solid electrolytes, fuel cells, band gaps for solar cells, and the ZT of thermoelectric materials with multiple-choice questions.
energy-materials.intro:
In lithium-ion batteries, Li⁺ shuttles between the crystals of the positive and negative electrodes during charge and discharge. Cathodes include layered rock salt LiCoO₂, spinel LiMn₂O₄ and olivine LiFePO₄, and the structure determines the dimensionality of the Li⁺ pathways, the voltage and the safety. The theoretical capacity of an electrode is Q = nF/(3.6M) mAh/g. Research is also advancing on all-solid-state batteries, which replace the liquid electrolyte with a solid electrolyte.
In fuel cells, whether the electrolyte conducts protons or oxide ions determines the operating temperature, and the theoretical emf of the hydrogen–oxygen reaction is about 1.23 V. The efficiency limit of solar cells is set by the balance between light transmission and thermalization losses, governed by the band gap of the absorber. The performance of thermoelectric materials is expressed by ZT = S²σT/κ, calling for materials that conduct electricity but not heat.

composites.name: Composite materials
composites.description: Learn the isostrain and isostress rules of mixtures for fiber-reinforced composites, volume fractions, CFRP and GFRP, critical fiber length, anisotropy of laminates, the role of the interface, and metal matrix and ceramic matrix composites with multiple-choice questions.
composites.intro:
Composite materials combine materials with different properties to obtain properties that none achieves alone. In fiber-reinforced plastics, strong, stiff fibers carry most of the load and the resin matrix transfers load to them. The Young's modulus parallel to the fibers is estimated by the isostrain rule of mixtures and perpendicular to them by the isostress rule, and unidirectional material differs greatly in stiffness by direction. It is therefore used as laminates stacked from plies with different orientations.
The interface joining fiber and matrix strongly affects performance. For short fibers, the critical fiber length is the length over which stress is transferred by interfacial shear, and glass fibers use coupling agents to strengthen adhesion. In ceramic matrix composites, on the other hand, the interface is deliberately made weak so that fiber pull-out raises toughness. Metal matrix composites are used to raise stiffness and wear resistance and to lower thermal expansion.

nanomaterials.name: Nanomaterials
nanomaterials.description: Check the relation between specific surface area and particle size, melting point depression of nanoparticles, the structure and properties of carbon nanotubes and graphene, quantum dots, synthesis methods for nanoparticles, agglomeration and dispersion, and BET specific surface area with multiple-choice questions, including calculations with explanations.
nanomaterials.intro:
As particles get smaller, the specific surface area increases in inverse proportion to size and, for spheres, can be estimated as S = 6/(ρd). As the fraction of surface atoms grows, surface energy starts to affect the properties of the whole material, and the melting point of metal nanoparticles falls below that of the bulk. In semiconductor quantum dots, confinement widens the effective band gap, so the emission color can be tuned by size. For carbon, graphene and the carbon nanotube, graphene rolled into a tube, are the representative examples.
Nanoparticles are made by top-down methods, which crush or carve larger materials, or by bottom-up methods, which assemble atoms and molecules through nucleation and growth. The key to uniform sizes is concentrating nucleation in a short time. The resulting particles agglomerate easily, so dispersion is maintained with surface charge or dispersants. Specific surface area is measured by the BET method, and comparing it with the TEM primary particle size and the size in liquid reveals the degree of agglomeration.

materials-selection.name: Materials selection and design
materials-selection.description: Learn Ashby materials selection charts, performance indices for light, stiff beams and light, strong ties, comparisons of cost and environmental impact, selecting materials to avoid fracture, and recyclability with multiple-choice questions, and practice calculations comparing mass and cost.
materials-selection.intro:
In Ashby's method, the design requirements are organized into function, constraints, objective and free variables, and eliminating the free variables yields a performance index, a combination of material properties alone. The materials that maximize E/ρ for a stiffness-limited tie, √E/ρ for a beam whose cross section can vary, ∛E/ρ for a plate whose thickness can vary, and σf/ρ for a strength-limited tie are favored. On a log–log selection chart of Young's modulus versus density, lines of constant performance index are straight, so candidates can be compared at a glance.
In real selection, besides performance, you also consider cost including the price per kg, the energy and CO₂ emissions from production to disposal, and whether a part avoids sudden fracture even with a crack (K_IC/σy). When objectives compete, the choice is made from the Pareto-optimal candidates using an exchange constant. Designing with fewer material types and easy disassembly, and controlling the elements that get mixed into scrap, are essential to improving recyclability.

magnetic-materials.name: Magnetic materials
magnetic-materials.description: Check the differences between diamagnetism, paramagnetism, ferromagnetism and ferrimagnetism, saturation magnetization calculations, domains and domain walls, single-domain particles and superparamagnetism, losses in soft magnetic materials, and the coercivity and maximum energy product of permanent magnets with multiple-choice questions.
magnetic-materials.intro:
The magnetism of a material is classified by how its atomic magnetic moments are arranged. Ferromagnets, in which the exchange interaction aligns the moments parallel, have a spontaneous magnetization even without an external field, but they split into many domains to lower the magnetostatic energy created by surface poles. During magnetization, domain walls move in weak fields and the magnetization inside the domains rotates in strong fields. Ferrimagnets (ferrites), in which the antiparallel moments of two sublattices do not cancel, are oxides with a high electrical resistance.
In applications, soft magnetic materials with small coercivity and low loss are used for transformer and motor cores, and hard magnetic materials (permanent magnets) with large coercivity and a large maximum energy product are used for the field magnets of motors and generators. In soft magnetic materials, magnetocrystalline anisotropy and magnetostriction are kept small, and eddy-current loss is suppressed by thin sheets and higher resistivity. In permanent magnets, a strong uniaxial magnetocrystalline anisotropy raises the coercivity. Small particles become single-domain, and even smaller ones become superparamagnetic.

processing.name: Materials processing and joining
processing.description: Learn about casting defects and precision casting, strain and force calculations for rolling, extrusion and deep drawing, springback, the carbon equivalent and heat input in welding, cold cracking and sensitization, solid-state joining, and sintering and HIP in powder metallurgy with multiple-choice questions.
processing.intro:
Metal parts are made by casting, in which metal is melted and poured into a mold; plastic working, in which the solid is deformed; welding and joining, which connect members; and powder metallurgy, in which powder is compacted and sintered. In casting, risers and the order of solidification are designed to prevent shrinkage cavities from solidification shrinkage and gas porosity. In plastic working such as rolling, forging, extrusion and deep drawing, dimensions and the forces needed are estimated using constant volume and true strain, and hot working can break up the cast structure and refine it.
In welding, a heat-affected zone forms around the melted region; in steel, hardening by rapid cooling and hydrogen-induced cold cracking are problems, and in stainless steel, sensitization by carbide precipitation. Cooling is managed through the carbon equivalent, heat input and preheating, and friction stir welding, which does not melt the material, is also used. In powder metallurgy, green compacts are sintered below the melting point, and dies are designed to allow for the dimensional shrinkage. It is essential for high-melting materials and cemented carbides, and remaining pores can be eliminated by hot isostatic pressing.

thermodynamics.name: Thermodynamics of materials
thermodynamics.description: Check the Gibbs energy and the condition for spontaneous change, how to read Ellingham diagrams, equilibrium oxygen partial pressures and H₂/H₂O ratios, activity and activity coefficients, the free energy of mixing of ideal and regular solutions, and spinodal decomposition with multiple-choice questions. Calculation questions come with worked explanations.
thermodynamics.intro:
At constant temperature and pressure, a change proceeds in the direction that lowers the Gibbs energy G = H − TS, and equilibrium is reached at ΔG = 0. The Ellingham diagram, which compares the stability of oxides, plots the ΔG° of formation per mol of O₂ against temperature; the lower its line, the more stable the oxide a metal forms, and that metal can reduce the oxides of the lines above. From ΔG° = RT ln pO₂, the equilibrium oxygen partial pressure at which a metal and its oxide coexist can be found.
Activity is the effective concentration of a component in a solution or solid solution; in an ideal solution it equals the mole fraction, and deviations are expressed by the activity coefficient. The free energy of a solid solution is set by the balance between the decrease due to the entropy of mixing and the enthalpy of mixing, and when unlike atoms repel each other in the regular solution model, a miscibility gap appears at low temperature. The equilibrium compositions of 2 phases are set by the common tangent, and spinodal decomposition occurs inside the gap.

biomaterials.name: Biomaterials
biomaterials.description: Learn about the idea of biocompatibility, bioinert, bioactive and bioresorbable ceramics, titanium and β titanium alloys, osseointegration, stress shielding and porous designs, superelasticity, and biodegradable polymers and magnesium with multiple-choice questions.
biomaterials.intro:
Biomaterials are materials that perform their function in contact with the body, inside it or on its surface. Biocompatibility is not a property decided by the material alone; it is judged by whether the material can work with an appropriate host response for its application. Ceramics are divided into bioinert materials such as alumina and zirconia, which hardly react in the body; hydroxyapatite and bioactive glass, which bond to bone; and β-TCP and others, which are resorbed and replaced by bone.
Implants that support bone use titanium and Ti-6Al-4V, which have excellent corrosion resistance and come into direct contact with bone, as well as Co-Cr alloys. When a metal far stiffer than bone carries the load, the stimulus to the bone falls and the bone thins, which is stress shielding, so β titanium alloys with a lower Young's modulus and porous metals have been developed. For parts that should disappear once their job is done, biodegradable polymers such as polylactic acid, which break down by hydrolysis, and magnesium alloys, which corrode in body fluids, are used.

fracture-fatigue.name: Fracture mechanics and fatigue
fracture-fatigue.description: Check Griffith theory, stress concentration and the plastic zone at a crack tip, fracture modes, reading fracture surfaces, fatigue crack initiation and growth, the Paris law, mean stress corrections and life estimates with Miner's rule through three-choice questions.
fracture-fatigue.intro:
The actual strength of materials is far below the theoretical strength because stress concentrates at the tips of tiny cracks. Griffith proposed that fracture proceeds when the elastic energy released as a crack extends exceeds the energy needed to create new surfaces. In metals, the work consumed by plastic deformation at the crack tip is far larger, and the tendency to fracture is organized in terms of the stress intensity factor K and its critical value.
Under repeated loading, cracks arise from slip at the surface even at stresses below the yield stress, and they advance a little in each cycle. The growth rate is set by the stress intensity factor range ΔK, and the intermediate region can be described by the Paris law. In design, the effect of mean stress is corrected with the Goodman diagram, and damage from varying loads is added up with Miner's rule to estimate life.

thermal-properties.name: Thermal properties of materials
thermal-properties.description: Learn the Dulong–Petit law and the Debye T³ law for heat capacity, the heat carriers in metals and insulators, the Wiedemann–Franz law, thermal diffusivity and its measurement, the origin of thermal expansion, Invar and materials that resist thermal shock through three-choice questions.
thermal-properties.intro:
Many thermal properties of solids can be explained by phonons, the quantized vibrations of atoms. The molar heat capacity of many elements near room temperature is about 3R, but at low temperatures vibrations become hard to excite, and the heat capacity of insulators shrinks in proportion to T³. Heat is carried mainly by conduction electrons in metals and by phonons in insulators, and the thermal conductivity of metals is linked to the electrical conductivity by the Wiedemann–Franz law.
While thermal conductivity expresses how easily heat flows in a steady state, thermal diffusivity α = κ/(ρc) expresses how quickly a change in temperature spreads, and it can be measured by the laser flash method. Thermal expansion arises from the asymmetry of the interatomic potential and is smaller in more strongly bonded materials. Against thermal shock, the cracking caused by sudden temperature changes, materials with smaller linear expansion coefficients are more resistant.

tribology.name: Surface treatment and tribology
tribology.description: Check the laws of friction and the real area of contact, adhesive and abrasive wear, the Archard wear equation, the Stribeck curve and lubrication regimes, solid lubrication, and carburizing, nitriding, electroless plating and hard coatings through three-choice questions.
tribology.intro:
In tribology, the study of friction and wear, the starting point is the real area of contact where tiny asperities on the surfaces touch. The real area of contact equals the load divided by the hardness and is far smaller than the apparent area, which explains why friction force is proportional to load and independent of contact area. Wear includes adhesive wear from adhesion at contact spots and abrasive wear from cutting by hard particles, and its amount is estimated from load and sliding distance with the Archard equation.
The lubrication regime shifts among boundary, mixed and hydrodynamic lubrication with oil viscosity, speed and pressure, as organized by the Stribeck curve. In surface treatment, carburizing and quenching or nitriding hardens the surface layer of steel, and electroless nickel plating and hard coatings such as TiN raise wear resistance. The key is to choose a method while considering how the treatment temperature affects the microstructure and dimensions of the base material.

glass-amorphous.name: Glasses and amorphous materials
glass-amorphous.description: Learn the short-range order and network structure of oxide glasses, network-forming and modifying oxides, non-bridging oxygens, the temperature dependence of viscosity, thermal tempering and chemical strengthening, how readily metallic glasses form and their properties, and amorphous silicon through three-choice questions.
glass-amorphous.intro:
Glass is an amorphous solid whose structure froze without crystallizing as the melt cooled; its nearest-neighbor coordination is uniform, but it has no long-range periodicity. In oxide glasses, network-forming oxides such as SiO₂ build a network of corner-sharing units, and modifying oxides such as Na₂O and CaO break bridges to create non-bridging oxygens, lowering the viscosity and the glass transition temperature. The temperature dependence of viscosity is described by the VFT equation and guides the temperatures for forming and annealing.
Glass breaks in tension from surface flaws, so it is strengthened by introducing compressive stress at the surface through thermal tempering or chemical strengthening by ion exchange. Metals, too, become glass even on slow cooling if the alloy has many components, atoms of different sizes and a negative heat of mixing, and such glasses show high strength and large elastic strain. Amorphous silicon with dangling bonds terminated by hydrogen is used in large-area thin-film transistors and solar cells.

high-temperature.name: High-temperature materials and creep
high-temperature.description: Check the three stages of the creep curve, power-law and diffusion creep, deformation mechanism maps, the Larson–Miller parameter, nickel-based superalloys and single-crystal blades, thermal barrier coatings, and high-temperature oxidation and protective scales through three-choice questions.
high-temperature.intro:
At high temperatures above about 0.4 times the melting point, creep, in which deformation proceeds with time even under a constant load, determines the life. The creep curve consists of three stages, transient, steady-state and accelerating, and design uses the steady-state creep rate. Power-law creep involving dislocation climb dominates at high stresses and diffusion creep at low stresses, and these fields are organized in a deformation mechanism map. Life is estimated with the Larson–Miller parameter, which combines temperature and time.
Jet engine turbine blades use nickel-based superalloys with a large amount of the ordered γ' phase precipitated, and single-crystal blades with no grain boundaries raise the creep strength. The surface is covered with a zirconia thermal barrier coating of low thermal conductivity to lower the metal temperature. In high-temperature oxidation, the parabolic law, in which diffusion through the scale controls growth, and the Pilling–Bedworth ratio serve as guides to protectiveness, and dense Cr₂O₃ and Al₂O₃ scales protect the alloy.

computational.name: Computational materials science
computational.description: Learn the ideas and limits of first-principles calculation (DFT), molecular dynamics and interatomic potentials, the Monte Carlo method, the CALPHAD method, the phase-field method, the finite element method and materials informatics through three-choice questions.
computational.intro:
In computational materials science, methods are chosen according to the scale of space and time to be handled. First-principles calculation (density functional theory, DFT), which starts from the electronic states, can obtain the structures and energies of up to a few hundred atoms without experimental data, but its approximations bring limits such as underestimating band gaps. Molecular dynamics, using interatomic potentials, follows the motion of many atoms for up to about nanoseconds, and the Monte Carlo method handles equilibrium states and long-time diffusion through probabilistic trials.
At the scale of microstructures and components, continuum methods take center stage. The CALPHAD method calculates multicomponent phase diagrams from Gibbs energy models of each phase, and the phase-field method follows changes in solidification and precipitation microstructures using diffuse interfaces. The finite element method finds the distributions of stress and temperature in components. Materials informatics, which predicts properties from data, has joined these, advancing materials development that combines computation and experiment.
